newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rejects Canadian airdrop plan for refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rejects Canadian airdrop plan for refugees.

text.p: Zaire rejected on Thursday a U.S.-backed Canadian plan to air-drop food for thousands of refugees and Zaireans fleeing fighting in the east of the country.
"The Zairean government is categorically opposed to the Canadian proposition to drop foodstuffs for refugees and displaced Zaireans," Information Minister Boguo Makeli said.
Boguo cited concern over the safety of the displaced people roaming the Zaire jungle and the fact that the airdrops would be staged from neighbouring countries it accuses of aggression.
Kinshasa has accused Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of aggression after a rebellion in two eastern provinces by ethnic Tutsi rebels who have seized a border strip.
"Zaire will not authorise overflights of its territory by any aircraft, whichever force it belongs to, for an operation so dangerous for the people concerned," Boguo told Reuters.
"It would be better to do nothing at all than treat refugees and displaced Zaireans like dogs."

The United Nations Security Council has approved the idea of a multinational force to protect refugees and secure food aid corridors. But support for the plan has been waning since more than half a million refugees the force was supposed to help returned to their homes in Rwanda earlier this month.
Canada, which is leading the U.N.-backed mission to help Rwandan and Burundian refugees in eastern Zaire, suggested this week that airdrops of food could be made in the area.
The United States said on Wednesday it supported a Canadian proposal to set up a headquarters in neighbouring Uganda for an international force to ease the refugee crisis.
U.S. airdrops to Hutu refugees in the area during the 1994 crisis were widely regarded as a waste of time and resources.
France which campaigned for intervention also backs the airlift plan.

Boguo spelt out his government's position as General Maurice Baril, the Canadian commander of the proposed multinational intervention force, arrived in Goma for talks with rebels who control much of the area.
Officials of the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR were also attending the talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
The Zaire government was likely to view such contacts as an affront on its national sovereignty, diplomats said.
Kabila, like his backers in neighbouring Rwanda, is against the presence of a multinational force in eastern Zaire on grounds that most Rwandan Hutu refugees had returned home.
